description_full: Walmart Inc. engages in the operation of retail and wholesale stores and clubs, ecommerce websites, and mobile applications worldwide. The company operates through three segments: Walmart U.S., Walmart International, and Sam's Club U.S. It operates supercenters, supermarkets, warehouse clubs, cash and carry stores, and discount stores under Walmart and Walmart Neighborhood Market brands; membership-only warehouse clubs; and ecommerce websites, such as walmart.com.mx, walmart.ca, flipkart.com, PhonePe and other sites. It offers grocery items, including dry grocery, snacks, dairy, meat, produce, deli and bakery, frozen foods, alcoholic and nonalcoholic beverages, as well as consumables, such as health and beauty aids, pet supplies, household chemicals, paper goods, and baby products; and fuel and other categories. In addition, it is involved in the provision of health and wellness products covering pharmacy, optical and hearing services, over-the-counter drugs, and protein and nutrition products; and home, hardlines, and seasonal items, including home improvement, outdoor living, gardening, furniture, apparel, jewelry, tools and power equipment, housewares, toys, and mattresses. Further, the company offers consumer electronics and accessories, software, video games, office supplies, appliances, and third-party gift cards. Additionally, it operates digital payment platforms; offers financial services and related products, including money transfers, bill payments, money orders, check cashing, prepaid access, co-branded credit cards, installment lending, and earned wage access; and markets lines of merchandise under private and licensed brands. The company was formerly known as Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. and changed its name to Walmart Inc. in February 2018. Walmart Inc. was founded in 1945 and is based in Bentonville, Arkansas.

financial_summary: Walmart Inc. is a mega-cap consumer defensive business with a $998.9B market cap on $713.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 18% against a 8% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $14.9B in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.90× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 44% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.8% (vs the 8% bar).

growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.3% over 3 years, 5.0% over 5 years and 4.0% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 31% of profits supports about 5.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -10.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 1.9x depreciation (3.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 7, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.

own: Insiders own 44.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 38%.

Shareholder yield is a modest 1.6% (0.8% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).

It has paid a dividend for 51 consecutive years, raising it 4.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 2,100,000 employees, each generates about $340K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 3.3% a year.
That works out to $7K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.6M (13x revenue per employee).
